rows.verified: HSE foundry COSHH guidance requires control of respirable crystalline silica and foundry fume exposure.
Ferrous foundry fume can cause lung cancer and other foundry fumes or spray mists can cause asthma and lung disease.
Dry casting sands, fettlings and kiln linings can generate respirable crystalline silica capable of causing silicosis.
Suitable molten-metal protective clothing is required where risk cannot be fully controlled by more effective measures.
Foundry risk assessment should verify building condition, clear routes, mould quality and dry furnace charge before relying on PPE.
Furnace work guidance identifies fume extraction as a core engineering control.
Foundry controls include maintained extraction, suitable respiratory protection, supervision, records and health surveillance.
Protective clothing selection must be supported by maintenance, training and supervision.
Foundry risk depends on metal, furnace, process, silica content, fume extraction, PPE, maintenance, competence and exposure duration.
HSE foundry evidence is process-, material-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
HSE lead guidance requires employers to assess and control occupational exposure to lead.
Lead in construction can occur in roof flashings, older paint and pipework and can cause serious health effects.
Occupational lead exposure can affect multiple body systems and requires prevention of harmful uptake.
Employers must identify lead hazards, assess exposure and implement suitable controls under the Control of Lead at Work Regulations.
Tasks producing lead dust or fume require particular attention during exposure assessment.
Workers are at higher risk when lead is heated, cut, blasted, sanded or otherwise converted to inhalable dust or fume.
Significant exposure determines whether enhanced controls and medical surveillance requirements apply.
Lead controls should be reviewed to confirm they remain effective and workers follow safe systems.
Lead risk depends on chemical form, task, airborne and ingestion pathways, exposure duration, hygiene, controls and worker susceptibility.
HSE lead evidence is substance-, task-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
